history Context for economic & labour KPIs above

These tiles mirror GDP, GDP per capita, GNI per capita (WDI), employment-to-population (15+), and modelled wage-style baselines where noted. Big synchronized moves often reflect global business cycles and commodity shocks.

Supportive phases

  • 1990s–2000s expansion — strong demand and trade growth in many regions.
  • 2010s recovery — repair after the GFC where policy space allowed.

Downside shocks

  • 2008–2009 GFC — GDP and employment hit together.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — output and jobs collapsed then rebounded unevenly.
  • 2022+ inflation & rates — weighed on real incomes and some labour markets.

history Context for health, housing-cost & energy KPIs

Life expectancy and birth rates follow WDI when merged; rent and gas are modelled but echo CPI and oil-market history.

Improved outcomes or relief

  • Public-health gains — secular rise in life expectancy in most countries.
  • 2014–2016 oil slump — cheaper retail fuel for importers for a time.

Pressure on households

  • Fertility transitions — policy and economics lower birth rates (e.g. China’s past one-child era).
  • 2021–2023 inflation — rent and energy squeezed real budgets.

history Context for environment, education, trade & internet KPIs

CO₂ and internet users align with WDI when loaded; education and trade balance mix WDI and modelled pieces.

Structural improvement

  • Renewables & efficiency (2010s+) — bend emissions trends where deployed.
  • Education expansion & ICT — rising attainment and connectivity.
  • Trade liberalization waves — deeper integration for many economies (1990s–2000s).

Setbacks

  • Coal-heavy growth — high per-capita CO₂ in several industrializers.
  • 2008–2009 & 2020 — trade and activity shocks visible in balances and output.

history Context for year-over-year changes

Short-run growth and emissions shifts are dominated by recessions, recoveries, energy prices, and weather-year effects—not a single narrative for every country.

Upswings

  • Reopening rebounds (2021) — partial snap-back after 2020 lockdowns.
  • Labour-market tightness (2021–2023) — employment gains in several economies.

Downswings

  • 2020 COVID year — negative GDP and employment in most countries.
  • Energy-price spikes — can raise nominal GDP volatility and hurt real wages.

history Context for the comparison table

Each column is the latest year in the series (after WDI merge). Cross-country rank changes mix real convergence, commodity luck, and methodology differences—read adjacent tab charts for full time paths.

When rankings improve

  • Reform & stabilization — sustained growth episodes (e.g. post-crisis recoveries).
  • Human development investment — schooling and health lift several columns together.

When rankings slip

  • Wars & state collapse — simultaneous damage to income, health, and connectivity.
  • Sudden stops & currency crises — GDP per capita and balances swing sharply.

history Context for long-horizon trend tiles

These summarize change from the first to the last year in the dashboard series. They mix WDI (GDP, life expectancy, CO₂ per capita when merged) with the same global history of shocks as the tab charts.

Long-run improvements (uneven)

  • Post-WWII reconstruction & Bretton Woods — income and trade recovery in much of the West.
  • 1990s–2000s globalization — catch-up growth for several emerging economies.
  • Medical progress — rising life expectancy in most countries over decades.

Repeated global setbacks

  • 1970s oil shocks & stagflation — slower growth and inflation.
  • 1980s debt crises — lost growth in many developing countries.
  • 2008–2009 GFC & 2020 COVID-19 — synchronized macro shocks.

history GDP & income per capita (WDI)

Documented macro shocks and expansions (IMF, World Bank, central banks) help explain synchronized dips and surges in output and GDP per capita—not precise year-by-year causality for every country.

Often supportive / expansionary

  • 1990s–2000s globalization & IT boom — trade integration and productivity gains in many economies (uneven).
  • Post–Cold War opening (early 1990s) — market access for several former planned economies.
  • 2010s recovery — rebound after the GFC where policy support restored demand (timing varied).

Often contractionary / volatile

  • 1973 & 1979 oil shocks — recessions and stagflation in many oil importers.
  • 1997–1998 Asian crisis — sharp currency and output collapses in several Asian economies.
  • 1998 Russia default — deep contraction and ruble stress.
  • 2008–2009 GFC — synchronized trade and GDP falls after the US credit shock.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — abrupt output drops from lockdowns and supply-chain breaks.
  • 2022+ energy & inflation shock — Ukraine war, sanctions, and commodity prices hit real incomes.

history Capital gains & valuations (modelled)

These series are illustrative, not official statistics. They still echo well-known episodes in equity and corporate-valuation history.

Often supported asset prices

  • 1980s–1990s bull markets — disinflation and equity gains in several advanced economies.
  • 2010s low-rate era — search for yield and rising multiples in many markets.

Often compressed valuations or gains

  • 2000 dot-com crash — sharp correction in tech-heavy indices.
  • 2008–2009 GFC — credit freeze and equity collapse, then uneven recovery.
  • 2020 Q1 crash & rebound — pandemic shock then policy-driven recovery.
  • 2022+ rate hikes — tighter financial conditions and pressure on growth-stock valuations.

history Defense budgets, burden-sharing & rearmament (modelled)

These are synthetic defense-spending series shaped to resemble major geopolitical eras: Cold War burden-sharing, the 1990s peace dividend, post-2001 expeditionary buildup, and the renewed rearmament cycle after 2014 and especially after 2022.

Common reasons spending rises

  • Cold War bloc competition — sustained high defense burdens across NATO, the USSR, and key Asian allies.
  • Post-2001 expeditionary campaigns — US-led operations lifted spending and procurement across several allies.
  • 2014 Crimea and 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine — European rearmament, munitions restocking, and higher burden-sharing targets.

Common reasons spending falls

  • 1990s peace dividend — many advanced economies cut force structure and procurement after the Soviet collapse.
  • Fiscal crises and austerity — debt stress often delayed replacement cycles and capital modernization.
  • Demographic and social spending pressures — aging populations can crowd out defense growth even when threats rise.

history Productivity, technology diffusion & stagnation (modelled)

This synthetic labour-productivity series tracks the familiar postwar pattern: catch-up growth, periodic efficiency plateaus, and faster gains where manufacturing upgrade, digital adoption, and capital deepening stayed strong.

Faster productivity growth

  • Export-led industrial upgrading — Korea, China, and later Malaysia improved output per worker through technology transfer and scale.
  • ICT and process innovation — 1990s–2000s software, logistics, and automation lifted high-income productivity frontiers.

Productivity slowdowns

  • Post-2008 stagnation — weak capital expenditure and low demand left many advanced economies with sluggish gains.
  • Resource or rent-heavy growth — GDP can rise without broad efficiency gains if output is driven by commodity booms or asset inflation.

history Employment & unemployment (WDI / ILO concepts)

WDI uses ILO-modelled labour indicators; national definitions still differ. Episodes below are standard in OECD and ILO narratives.

Tighter labour markets

  • Mid-late 1990s expansion — falling unemployment in several OECD economies.
  • 2010s job recovery — repair after the GFC as demand returned (uneven by skill and region).

Job losses / higher unemployment

  • Early 1980s recessions — anti-inflation policy and rising joblessness.
  • Early 1990s transition recessions — restructuring in former Eastern Bloc countries.
  • 1997–1998 emerging-market crises — joblessness with currency stress.
  • 2008–2010 Great Recession — sharp rises in unemployment and underemployment.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — spikes in joblessness or furloughs where services locked down.

history National income per capita (WDI) & labour income context

The Jobs tab line chart shows GNI per capita (Atlas method) from WDI when the API loads—a macro income measure, not employer-reported wages. Pay inequality and composition still follow the same broad cycles as employment.

Phases often linked to real wage gains

  • 1990s–2000s convergence — strong pay growth in several emerging economies with export-led growth.
  • Post-2020 tight labour markets — nominal wage pressure in some sectors where labour was scarce.

Phases often linked to stagnation or cuts

  • 1970s stagflation — real wages eroded where inflation outpaced nominal deals.
  • 2008–2012 — freezes or declines during and after the GFC in several countries.
  • 2021–2023 inflation — where pay lagged prices, real earnings fell temporarily.

history Food & rent (modelled)

Commodity and housing markets drive these costs; CPI and FAO food indices document the real episodes below.

Downward pressure (sometimes)

  • 1980s–1990s disinflation — slower nominal price growth after the 1970s.
  • Stable harvest periods — lower food volatility in major exporters (not universal).

Upward pressure

  • 2000s commodity super-cycle — sustained food and energy pressure before the GFC.
  • 2021–2023 inflation — supply chains, stimulus, and war lifted food and shelter costs in many economies.

history Housing & electricity (modelled)

House prices and power tariffs reflect credit conditions, regulation, and wholesale energy markets.

Improved affordability or access (context-dependent)

  • Post-2008 buyer markets — price corrections in several bubble markets.
  • Renewable scale-up (2010s+) — in some grids, cheaper marginal electricity (policy-dependent).

Strain on households

  • 2008–2012 housing bust — negative equity and wealth shocks where bubbles burst.
  • 2022+ energy crisis — wholesale power and gas spikes after the Ukraine war (region-dependent).

history Transport fuel & vehicles (modelled)

Pump prices track crude oil, taxes, and exchange rates; vehicle markets follow credit cycles.

Cheaper motoring (sometimes)

  • 2014–2016 oil slump — lower retail fuel in importing countries.
  • Brief 2020 demand shock — short-lived fuel price dips during lockdowns.

More expensive transport

  • 1973 & 1979 oil shocks — large retail fuel increases.
  • 2022+ — war-related energy spike and volatility at the pump.

history Phone & internet contract costs (modelled)

Phone costs transition from flat landline fees toward rising mobile/data plans through the 1990s–2010s. Broadband barely existed before 1993; dial-up gave way to DSL, cable, then fibre. Deregulation dynamics differ sharply between markets.

Competition driving prices down

  • France 2012 — Iliad (Free Mobile) — disruptive market entry slashed mobile prices; similar dynamics later in UK and Nordics.
  • South Korea & Japan broadband investment (2000s) — government-backed fibre build-outs drove down per-Mb costs sharply.

Prices remaining high

  • North American mobile markets — limited operator competition kept USD plan prices well above comparable European tariffs.
  • Data plan inflation (2010s+) — shift from voice-only to unlimited-data contracts drove average revenue per user upward.

history TV & total connectivity bundle costs (modelled)

Pay TV expanded from a US-centric model in the 1970s to global cable through the 1990s. Streaming disruption created new subscription layers; remaining cable subscribers often paid more as audience bases shrank.

Consumer savings possible

  • Cord-cutting wave (2015+) — households replacing expensive cable with one or two streaming services initially saved meaningfully.
  • Public-broadcasting models — Nordic and continental European licence-fee structures kept TV costs lower than North American bundles.

Bundle creep

  • Streaming fragmentation (2020s) — multiple subscriptions pushed monthly totals back toward old cable-era levels.
  • Live sports rights escalation — premium sport remained the anchor sustaining high video bundle prices.

history Health spending (WDI) & food banks (modelled)

Per-capita health expenditure follows WDI when merged; food-bank series remain illustrative.

Expanded protection or treatment

  • Universal coverage expansion — social-insurance and tax-funded systems broadened access in many middle- and high-income countries.
  • Post-1990 medical technology gains — new drugs, diagnostics, and chronic-disease management lifted spending and coverage together.

Strain on households & charities

  • 2008–2012 austerity — service cuts and rising food-bank use in some regions.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — income loss and surging emergency food demand in many countries.

history Housing tenure & population age (mixed sources)

Homeownership shifts with credit, urbanization, and policy; median age rises with longevity and falling fertility.

Homeownership or stability

  • Post-war suburban growth — rising owner-occupation in several Western countries.
  • Healthy longevity — older populations reflect medical progress (also a fiscal challenge).

Pressure on tenure or youth

  • 2008 housing crash — foreclosures and tenure shifts in bubble markets.
  • High-price cities (2010s+) — delayed household formation and renting longer.

history Education & literacy (WDI)

Secondary gross enrollment and adult literacy (WDI when merged) reflect school expansion and literacy campaigns; conflict destroys schooling. Gross enrollment can exceed 100%.

Human capital gains

  • Universal schooling drives — especially East Asia and Latin America in late 20th century.
  • Post-colonial investment — literacy gains in many African and Asian countries (uneven).

Setbacks

  • 1990s transition crises — disrupted education spending in parts of the former USSR.
  • 2010s–2020s conflicts — Syria, Yemen, and others: lost years of schooling.

history DEI, gender parity & subjective wellbeing (modelled)

These composite indices are illustrative. The DEI line is a broad proxy for diversity, equity, and inclusion conditions, while gender equality and happiness capture narrower but related social outcomes.

Inclusion & wellbeing

  • 1990s–2000s anti-discrimination and parity reforms — education, hiring, and civic-rights rules widened formal inclusion in many countries.
  • Post-apartheid South Africa and multicultural-policy states — civil-rights expansion widened representation, even where inequality persisted.

Stress on reported wellbeing

  • 2008–2012 austerity — cuts and labour-market stress can weaken the lived experience of equity even when formal rights stay in place.
  • Polarization and post-2020 backlash cycles — representation can improve on paper while social trust and belonging become more contested.

history Political rights & security (modelled)

Use V-Dem, Freedom House, or UNODC for rigorous cross-country measures; this block ties narrative to regime change and conflict.

Liberalization episodes

  • 1989–1991 transitions — multiparty systems in much of Central/Eastern Europe.
  • 1980s–1990s Latin American democratization — civilian rule after military regimes.

Repression & violence

  • 1994 Rwanda genocide — extreme violence and state collapse.
  • 2010s–2020s MENA & other wars — humanitarian catastrophe and rights erosion in conflict zones.

history Birth & death rates (WDI)

Crude rates respond to cohort size, policy, epidemics, and war—standard in UN demographic yearbooks.

Demographic dividend phases

  • Falling mortality (1970s–2000s) — child survival gains lowered death rates in many countries.
  • Later fertility decline — fewer births as education and contraception spread.

Mortality or birth shocks

  • 1990s Russia — rising deaths amid economic and health-system stress.
  • HIV/AIDS (1980s–2000s) — death-rate spikes where treatment was unavailable.
  • COVID-19 — excess mortality waves in 2020–2022.

history Life expectancy & fertility (WDI)

Longevity rises with public health; total fertility falls with female education and urbanization.

Health & family transitions

  • Antiretroviral scale-up — life-expectancy recovery in high-HIV countries.
  • China’s development decades — rapid mortality decline and then fertility fall.

Setbacks

  • China one-child era — structurally low fertility with long-run aging.
  • Post-Soviet mortality crisis — life-expectancy drops before partial recovery.

history Reproductive health: abortion & infant mortality

Infant mortality is WDI-backed when available; abortion rates here are modelled. Both respond to reproductive healthcare access, maternal health, contraception, law, and household conditions, but they do not move one-for-one.

Better reproductive-health systems

  • Contraception and prenatal-care expansion — fewer unsafe pregnancies, lower maternal risk, and better infant outcomes.
  • Vaccines, ORS, and neonatal care — the classic drivers of the long global decline in infant mortality documented by WHO and UNICEF.

Access gaps or policy shocks

  • Conflict, clinic disruption, and poverty — reproductive-health access and infant outcomes both worsen when systems break down.
  • Restrictive law or poor contraception access — official abortion rates can fall while unsafe procedures or unwanted births rise.

history Obesity & smoking (modelled)

Nutrition transition and tobacco control shape these curves; WHO reports country-level survey trends.

Public-health progress

  • WHO FCTC (2005+) — taxes, packaging, and smoke-free laws cut smoking in many countries.
  • Child nutrition programs — slower obesity growth where policy intervened early.

Risk increases

  • Ultra-processed diets & sedentary work — rising obesity in middle-income countries.
  • 1990s–2000s tobacco marketing — uptake in emerging markets before regulation.

history Diabetes & mental health (modelled)

NCD prevalence rises with obesity and aging; mental-health indices in surveys spiked around COVID-19.

Better management

  • Primary-care screening (2000s+) — earlier diabetes detection in some systems.
  • Digital mental-health access — expanded reach in OECD countries post-2020.

Worsening stressors

  • Diabetes linked to obesity epidemic — parallel rise in many regions.
  • COVID-19 lockdowns — documented anxiety/depression surges in national health surveys.

history CO₂ & renewable energy (WDI)

Industrial coal and oil raised emissions; policy and cheap renewables bend the curve where deployed at scale.

Decarbonization drivers

  • EU ETS & national carbon rules (2005+) — priced emissions in participating economies.
  • Post-2015 Paris & subsidy phase-out — renewable share gains in many grids.

Emissions pressure

  • Coal-heavy industrialization — rapid CO₂ growth in several emerging economies (1970s–2010s).
  • 2022+ coal rebounds — some countries delayed phase-outs for energy security.

history Forest & water (WDI forest; water modelled)

Forest area reflects land-use policy and commodity demand; water-quality composites need national environmental monitoring.

Conservation & recovery

  • China afforestation programs — net forest gains in official land-cover data (debated quality).
  • EU & US stabilization — forest area flat or rising in some periods.

Deforestation & pollution stress

  • Amazon & tropical clearing (1980s–2000s) — large forest loss for agriculture.
  • Industrial effluent & runoff — water stress in fast-growing regions (national data vary).

history Internet & mobile (WDI)

ICT adoption accelerated after commercial internet and GSM; policy and competition shaped prices and coverage.

Adoption booms

  • 1990s internet & GSM rollout — steep user curves in OECD and many emerging markets.
  • 2007+ smartphones — mobile data and apps as default access path.

Digital divide

  • Rural & low-income gaps — persistent where infrastructure or affordability lagged.
  • COVID-19 — exposed households without devices or broadband for remote school/work.

history Broadband speed & R&D (modelled + WDI R&D)

Fiber and cable upgrades lift measured Mbps; R&D intensity reflects innovation policy and industrial structure.

Innovation & connectivity

  • 2010s fiber & 4G/5G — faster consumer broadband in leading markets.
  • R&D targets (EU, East Asia) — public and private science spending as % of GDP.

Volatility & cuts

  • 2000–2001 dot-com crash — telecom capex and equity valuations fell sharply.
  • Austerity (2010s) — science budgets flat or down in some countries.

history Exports & imports (WDI)

Goods and services trade rises with globalization and falls in global recessions; commodity exporters swing with prices.

Trade expansion

  • Uruguay Round & WTO (1995) — lower barriers and dispute rules.
  • Global value chains (1990s–2000s) — fragmented production across Asia, Europe, Americas.
  • China’s WTO entry (2001) — export and import surge.

Trade collapses

  • 2008–2009 — synchronized trade drop in the GFC.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — services trade and travel collapsed; goods volatile.
  • 2018–2019 tariffs — US–China bilateral diversion.

history Trade balance (exports minus imports)

Surpluses and deficits reflect savings/investment balances, commodity prices, and exchange rates—not “good” or “bad” alone.

Improved external positions (sometimes)

  • 1990s EM export booms — manufacturing-led surpluses or smaller deficits.
  • Post-shock adjustment — import compression after crises temporarily widens surplus.

Large deficits or volatility

  • 1970s oil importers — wider deficits with energy bills.
  • 2022+ terms-of-trade shock — energy and food importers saw balance pressure.
  • Sanctions (2022+) — forced rerouting of trade and payment channels.

history Legal & irregular migration (modelled)

Use UN DESA, OECD, and national immigration statistics for policy work; these charts are illustrative. Denominators for per-capita charts use WDI population when merged.

This dashboard does not validate bilateral origin-country flows, so it cannot tell you exactly where migrants came from each year. For that question, use bilateral UN/OECD/IOM datasets. What it can show is the demographic effect of migration: population growth, changes in the working-age share, pressure on schools and housing, and shifts in age diversity.

Demographic gains

  • Young inflows — can slow population aging and support labor supply.
  • Family and skilled-worker migration — often raises school-age and working-age cohorts.

Adjustment pressures

  • Rapid inflows — can strain housing, schools, and integration services.
  • Large refugee waves — change local age structure and dependency ratios quickly.

history Migration per 100k population

Per-capita flows scale raw counts by population; the same absolute inflow looks larger for small countries. Policy regimes (visas, asylum rules) dominate year-to-year changes.

The native/immigration ratio chart is an annual inflow ratio: (legal + irregular inflows) / resident population x 100. It is not a stock share of all foreign-born residents.

Integration & regularization

  • Regularization waves — legal status for long-term residents (varies by country).
  • Points systems — selection aligned with labour demand in several OECD states.

Crisis-driven surges

  • 1990s Balkans — refugee inflows into neighboring states.
  • US southern border (2010s–2020s) — high policy salience; use DHS/CBP official series for counts.

history Quality of Life & Happiness

Data caveat: Composite QoL indices (Numbeo et al.) and the World Happiness Report only exist from the 2000s and 2012 respectively. Values shown before those dates are backward extrapolations based on known 1990 anchors and country-specific trends — they are illustrative, not sourced. Both measures improve with sustained development but diverge sharply during crises.

Drivers of improvement

  • Economic growth + public services — rising incomes and better infrastructure lift both composites together.
  • East Asian catch-up (1990s–2010s) — rapid gains in China, Korea, and Malaysia.

Divergences & declines

  • 1990s post-Soviet transition — life satisfaction collapsed in Russia and former Soviet bloc despite GDP rebounds.
  • 2020 COVID-19 — happiness and QoL dipped simultaneously in most countries; recovery uneven.

history Human Development & Inequality

HDI combines income, education, and life expectancy into a single score; Gini captures how evenly income is distributed within a country (higher = more unequal). Countries can grow richer while inequality widens.

Development gains

  • Universal education & healthcare investment — lifted HDI in many developing countries from 1970s onward.
  • Brazil Bolsa Família (2003+) — targeted transfers helped compress the Gini from extreme highs.

Inequality pressures

  • China's market transition (1990s+) — rapid growth paired with sharply rising Gini as coastal cities pulled ahead.
  • Global capital income gap (2000s+) — returns to capital outpacing wages in many OECD countries.

history Governance: Corruption & Political Freedom

Data caveat: Transparency International's CPI only exists since 1995; Freedom House scores since 1972 with methodology changes. Pre-1995 corruption and pre-1991 political freedom values are backward-modelled estimates anchored to 1990 baselines. Soviet-bloc and revolutionary-era authoritarian floors (1970–1991) are approximated explicitly. Treat all pre-1995 governance data as illustrative.

Governance improvements

  • South Korea anti-corruption reforms (2000s+) — independent prosecution and civil society pressure cut bribery.
  • EU accession conditionality (1990s–2000s) — rule-of-law requirements pushed candidate countries to reform.

Governance setbacks

  • 1990s Russia — privatization era spawned oligarchic capture and severe corruption.
  • Democratic backsliding (2010s) — freedom scores fell in Hungary, Turkey, and several other mid-income countries.

history Free speech, press culture & media trust (modelled)

This block separates the institutional environment for speech from trust in old and new media. From 2012 onward, trust ratings are anchored to the Edelman Trust Barometer (traditional media vs. search engines + social media). Pre-2012 values are modelled. Trust can fall even in free systems when polarization rises.

Open information environments

  • Constitutional protections and independent courts — high free-speech scores are sustained where journalists and critics face fewer legal threats.
  • Strong public broadcasters — Nordic and some Commonwealth systems preserved relatively high trust in legacy news for longer.

Polarization or repression

  • State censorship and platform controls — lower free-speech scores in tightly managed information systems.
  • Disinformation waves (2010s+) — both legacy and digital trust can weaken when audiences sort into partisan ecosystems.

history Attention shift: legacy to digital media (modelled)

These series model the transition from print, broadcast, and cable dominance toward digital-first platforms, streaming, creator ecosystems, and algorithmic distribution. Market share here means share of audience attention and ad-revenue mix, not legal ownership concentration.

Digital opportunity

  • Lower publishing barriers — new media expanded voice, niche reporting, and creator-led formats after the web and smartphone era.
  • Mobile-first adoption — emerging markets often leapfrogged directly into digital news and video consumption.

Legacy erosion & platform dependence

  • Print advertising collapse — newsroom layoffs and local-news deserts followed the shift of ad budgets to platforms.
  • Algorithmic concentration — digital market share can be high while editorial independence narrows around a few dominant gateways.

history Health System Access: Wait Times & Physician Density

Elective surgery wait times are a proxy for public system capacity; physician density (WB indicator SH.MED.PHYS.ZS) tracks health workforce supply. High-income single-payer systems often face queues the US fee-for-service model avoids—at a price.

System capacity gains

  • Post-war hospital building (1950s–1980s) — most OECD countries expanded beds and trained more physicians.
  • Korea & UAE investment (1990s–2010s) — rapid growth in physician numbers from a low base.

System stress

  • COVID-19 surgical backlogs (2020–2023) — elective procedures deferred globally; waits surged, especially in NHS-style systems.
  • Austerity (2010–2015) — health workforce hiring freezes in several European countries.

history Hospital Capacity & Healthcare Spending

Bed counts reflect historic hospital-building eras (Japan, Russia still carry Soviet-era density) and now-dominant moves toward outpatient care. Spending per capita can rise without proportional outcome gains if prices, not utilization, drive costs.

Capacity expansion

  • Korea & China (1990s–2010s) — dramatic bed growth as economies urbanised and middle classes demanded hospital care.
  • Health spending growth — OECD countries consistently increased real per-capita expenditure.

Rationalisation & pressure

  • OECD bed reduction (1980s+ onwards) — shift to day surgery and community care cut inpatient stays.
  • US spending outlier — highest per-capita spending with average life expectancy among peers.

history Christian & Muslim Population Shares (modelled)

These are illustrative long-run trajectories based on Pew Research demographic projections and national census data. Religious identity changes slowly via births, deaths, immigration, and voluntary switching (secularisation). Year-to-year precision is low.

Broad trends

  • Christian share declining in Western Europe & North America — secularisation and immigration diversification from the 1970s onward.
  • Muslim share growing in Western Europe — immigration from MENA and South Asia; higher birth rates in the first generation.

Limitations to note

  • Census methodology varies — self-identification vs. state religion registration produces different totals.
  • UAE & Malaysia — high Muslim share reflects indigenous majority (Malaysia) and expatriate composition (UAE).

history Secular & Eastern Traditions (modelled)

Secularisation is among the most consistent long-run social trends in high-income countries; the "nones" (no religion) are a fast-growing category in surveys. Hindu and Buddhist shares are relatively stable regionally but shift with diaspora migration patterns.

Secularisation wave

  • Nordic countries — very high secular share by 2000s; cultural Christianity without formal belief.
  • South Korea — uniquely high and rising "no religion" share alongside both Christianity and Buddhism.

Regional contrasts

  • India — Hindu majority extremely stable at ~80%; communal politics shape official identity data.
  • Japan — high "secular" in surveys but Buddhist & Shintō practices remain embedded in life-cycle rituals.

Media trust sources: Values from 2012 onward are anchored to the Edelman Trust Barometer (traditional media vs. search engines + social media). Pre-2012 points are backward-modelled. See also the Quality of Life tab for market-share trends.
